name: Approach for proximal femoral nailing
corridor: Proximal gluteal split several centimeters above the greater-trochanter tip, along the posterior bowed femoral axis, to an implant-specific trochanteric start

positioning.text: Position supine or lateral so the pelvis and greater trochanter are accessible and true AP and lateral images of the proximal femur can be obtained.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the tip of the greater trochanter and the femoral axis, using the image intensifier when habitus obscures palpation.

incision.text: Make a 3–5 cm incision several centimeters proximal to the greater-trochanter tip on the proximal extension of the bowed femoral axis, which lies somewhat posterior to a purely lateral line; shift the portal with soft-tissue thickness and the insertion handle.

superficial_interval.text: Incise the gluteal fascia 3–8 cm longitudinally and split gluteal fibers by blunt dissection to the trochanter tip.

deep_interval.text: Identify the trochanter tip with a finger or instrument and place the entry according to the selected nail; most trochanteric-fracture nails enter through the greater trochanter rather than the trochanteric fossa.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, gluteal fascia, longitudinal gluteal split, trochanteric cortex, then the femoral canal.

structures_at_risk.text: The posterior femoral shaft cortex, abductor muscle, and an eccentric canal track are at risk if the incision and instruments do not follow the bowed femoral axis.

danger_zones.text: A too-anterior or off-axis incision promotes eccentric reaming or posterior cortical perforation, especially with long nails.

retraction_hazards.text: Do not lever instruments against the trochanter to compensate for a poorly aligned skin portal; keep the working path collinear with the canal.

exposure.text: Provides a proximal portal for implant-specific trochanteric-entry nailing without opening the fracture.

limitations.text: The exact start depends on nail design, and flexion or abduction deformity of the proximal fragment can hide the desired entry until the fragment is realigned.

indications.text: Used to insert trochanteric-entry intramedullary nails for trochanteric fractures after the proximal femur is aligned.

closure.text: Repair fascia without tethering abductors and close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include eccentric reaming, posterior femoral cortical perforation, and a poorly seated nail from an incorrect implant-specific start.

procedure_applications.condition: A cephalomedullary nail with a greater-trochanter entry is selected for a trochanteric or pertrochanteric fracture

questions.question: Where do most nails designed for trochanteric fractures enter?
questions.answer: Through the greater trochanter, not the trochanteric fossa; the precise point is implant-specific.

questions.question: Why is the incision placed somewhat posterior along the femoral bow?
questions.answer: So instruments and the nail travel along the canal and do not perforate the posterior cortex.

questions.question: How can a flexed or abducted proximal fragment be realigned to find the start?
questions.answer: With a percutaneous Schanz screw and/or a ball-spiked pusher.
